pitch.short: I started a student stationery subscription and wound it down when the postage ate the margin, spent three years in sales operations at Pinewick Paper & Print where I re-cut the sales territories, and built the quote approval desk at Tamarack Packaging.
why_hire: I have run a small business end to end. Desk Drawer Co shipped 1,480 boxes and took $41,400 in sales before I closed it and wrote up why.
I fix the number a team argues about. At Pinewick I re-cut four territories into five, and reps at or above quota went from 5 of 12 to 9 of 12 within two quarters.
I build processes that outlast me. In my Tamarack internship I set up a quote approval desk, and quotes sent the same day rose from 34% to 81%. They still use it.
pitch.for_company_template: Why {company}: I want to sit between sales and finance at {company}, keep the forecast honest and own the handoff that most often goes wrong.

about.intro: I grew up in Harlow Ridge and studied commerce at Brindle Hollow College. In my first year a friend and I started Desk Drawer Co, a stationery subscription box for students. It shipped 1,480 boxes in 21 months, and then I closed it because every box mailed outside town lost money. In 2022 I joined Pinewick Paper & Print in Larchmont Falls as a sales operations analyst, and in 2024 I became sales operations manager under regional manager Gordie Pruitt, who owns a lot of motivational posters. In 2025 I started a PGDM at Ashgrove School of Management, and this spring I did a ten-week internship at Tamarack Packaging. Every number below carries a note on its source.
about.now: I am finishing the PGDM and writing The Quote Desk, a newsletter for people who run sales operations. I also keep a free pricing sheet for small print shops, and Dennis Hale from Pinewick accounting has approved its rounding.

quote-calculator.context: Over a year at Pinewick I watched small print shops in the valley phone our order desk to ask what a job should cost. I built them a pricing sheet in my spare time.
quote-calculator.problem: Most shops priced on the back of an envelope, forgot waste and setup time, and rounded in whichever direction felt friendly.
what_i_did: Built a Google Sheets template that takes paper, ink, setup time and waste and returns a price with a margin.
Put Dennis Hale's rounding rules in as the default and asked him to check them (he found one error, which he mentioned several times).
Added a short Apps Script menu to save each quote as a PDF.
Shared it with print shops through two trade groups and fixed the questions they sent back.

decisions.choice: Keep it as a plain spreadsheet
decisions.why: Shop owners already know Sheets, and none wanted a login for a tool that does arithmetic.

decisions.choice: Round up to the next 5 cents on every line
decisions.why: Rounding each line instead of the total kept the sheet easy to check by hand, which is how Dennis would have checked it anyway.

quote-calculator.learned: Owners trusted the sheet once they saw the formulas, so I stopped hiding them.
quote-calculator.next: Add a paper price table that shops can update each quarter.

reorder-reminder.context: The Ashgrove School of Management venture course gave each team two months to choose a problem, try out a product and present it on final-pitch night. My team of four chose small offices that buy paper and toner from suppliers near Larchmont Falls.
reorder-reminder.problem: Office managers notice they are out of paper when the printer stops, and then phone the supplier to ask for a rush delivery.
what_i_did: Ran the team and divided the two months into research, prototype and pitch.
Held 27 interviews with office managers and three with suppliers (own record).
Built a clickable prototype in Glide that tracks stock per office and sends a restock prompt on WhatsApp.
Ran a three-week pilot with 5 offices using the prototype (own record).
Pitched on final-pitch night and came 2nd of 22 teams.

decisions.choice: Use WhatsApp prompts, not a new app
decisions.why: Every office manager we met already used WhatsApp for supplier chat, and none wanted another login.

decisions.choice: Start with paper and toner only
decisions.why: Those two items run out most often and are reordered on a regular cycle, so a three-week pilot was long enough to see a result.

reorder-reminder.learned: Offices tried it only once their regular supplier recommended it. A real rollout should begin with the suppliers.

account-profitability.context: An Ashgrove School of Management live project with Halloran Box & Crate, a corrugated box maker in Larchmont Falls that sells to nine groups of customers, from local bakeries to regional distributors.
account-profitability.problem: The company only had one overall margin figure, so it could not see which customer groups made money after freight, rush fees and discounts.
account-profitability.my_role: Team member, 3 people; built the account margin model
what_i_did: Pulled twelve months of invoice and freight data from the company's accounting exports.
Built a margin view for each of the nine customer groups: price, material, freight, rush fees and discounts.
Found two groups losing money on every order once freight and rush fees were counted.
Presented the model to the owner with one recommendation per group.

decisions.choice: Split shared plant costs by machine hours
decisions.why: Presses are shared across groups. Machine hours kept the comparison fair, and the owner could verify it himself.

decisions.choice: Give each group its own fix, not only a price rise
decisions.why: One losing group had steady volume and lost money only through rush fees, so a cap on rush orders was cheaper than losing the customers.

account-profitability.learned: The owner moved inside a week since every row closed with a call that was his to make.

the-quote-desk.context: I started The Quote Desk in September 2025, during the PGDM, to learn how other sales operations teams run quoting and forecasting.
the-quote-desk.problem: Most writing on sales operations is general advice. I wanted the real intake form and rule sheet from people who handle quotes every day.
what_i_did: Send an issue out every second week, each centred on a talk with a sales operations lead.
Ask each guest to share their working quote form, their rule sheet and one habit they dropped.
Interviewed 16 operators so far (own record).
Grew the list to 1,400 subscribers without paid promotion (own record).

decisions.why: A real process from one team teaches readers more than a list of general tips.

decisions.choice: Every two weeks, not every week
decisions.why: Booking a guest takes me a week and writing the piece takes another, so a weekly schedule would have meant rushed issues.

the-quote-desk.learned: Readers passed along the issues that showed a guest's actual form, so I request it before we talk.

quote-approval-desk.context: Tamarack Packaging is a Larchmont Falls maker of shipping cartons and mailers. By 2026 it had nine sales reps and a head of sales, Odalys Brennan, who was tired of hearing about quotes that went stale.
quote-approval-desk.problem: A discounted quote went through email to three people. It took about three days, and only 34% of quotes went out the same day they were requested.
quote-approval-desk.my_role: Revenue Operations Intern; owned the desk and the discount rules
what_i_did: Traced 60 quotes from request to send and logged where each one waited. 52% of the delay was people asking who was allowed to approve.
Wrote 17 discount rules with the head of sales and finance, each with one approver.
Replaced the email chain with one intake form and a shared queue, with a four-hour response window.
Posted the queue to Slack each morning and each afternoon so nothing aged quietly.
Trained all nine reps in two short sessions and took questions for the first month.

decisions.choice: Settle who approves before building anything
decisions.why: Most of the wait was uncertainty about authority. Once each rule had one approver, the form was simple.
Discounts under 5% made up most of the queue and almost never changed. Letting reps send them removed a third of the work.

results.note: mean of the final month on site; leadership-confirmed, not audited
8 weeks, from the queue log; own record

quote-approval-desk.learned: The form took one week; agreeing the rules took three. The desk only worked once the head of sales stopped approving quotes by text message.
quote-approval-desk.next: Add a monthly review of discount rules that were never used.

order-desk-tracker.context: In 2023 I was a Sales Operations Analyst in Pinewick's order desk team, following each customer order from confirmation to dispatch.
order-desk-tracker.problem: Order status lived in five spreadsheets, a clipboard and Tilly Brandt's memory. A stuck order often had no clear owner, and the median time from confirmation to dispatch was 5.6 days.
order-desk-tracker.my_role: Sales Operations Analyst; designed and built the tracker
what_i_did: Walked the path from confirmation to dispatch with two order desk leads and marked each point where orders sat idle.
Put every order in a single Airtable base, each row carrying a stage, a named owner and the next action.
Set a Zapier rule that pings Slack whenever an order stays at one stage beyond two days.
Retired the five old spreadsheets, kept the clipboard for Wendell Odom, and helped two more teams set up the tracker.

decisions.choice: Use Airtable and Zapier rather than queueing an IT ticket
decisions.why: IT had a backlog of about three months. The no-code build went live within five weeks, and the desk leads could adjust it without asking anyone.
Orders stalled mostly at handoffs, where each person believed the next one was chasing.

results.note: sales, warehouse and accounting; own record

territory-realignment.context: In 2023 Pinewick's four sales territories in the Northern Valley had not been changed in nine years. Gordie Pruitt asked whether a fairer split would help more reps reach quota.
territory-realignment.problem: There was no account map. Some reps covered far more accounts than they could visit, others had thin patches, and nobody could say how many accounts had gone untouched.
territory-realignment.my_role: Sales Operations Analyst, then Manager; led the re-cut
what_i_did: Mapped 1,240 active accounts by town, size and buying cycle and scored each rep's real workload.
Drew five territories with equal workload and agreed the draft with Gordie and the 12 reps, one account list at a time.
Ran the handover with a one-page brief for each moved account, written with the old rep.
Reviewed 90-day contact gaps every month and called the reps who had accounts with no touch.
Wrote the account scoring rules down, so the next re-cut would not start from scratch.

decisions.why: Equal revenue meant equal luck. Equal visit workload meant every rep had a fair chance to reach quota.

decisions.choice: Let reps keep up to five accounts they had a long history with
decisions.why: It cost little in balance and removed most of the objections, including a long one from Marla Finch.

results.note: from the CRM export; own record

territory-realignment.learned: Reps accepted the new map when they saw their own account list first. The map was never the hard part; the order of the conversations was.

forecast-playbook.context: After the territory re-cut, Gordie wanted quarterly forecasts he could trust. Until then the forecast was built in a regional meeting that ran on whiteboard acronyms.
forecast-playbook.problem: The quarterly forecast was off by 19%, and the reasons sat in my sheets and the reps' memories.
forecast-playbook.my_role: Sales Operations Manager; wrote the playbook
what_i_did: Reviewed 80 closed deals from the past year and coded why each one slipped, moved or closed early.
Wrote the forecast playbook: stage definitions, the evidence a deal needs at each stage and a weekly check.
Set a rule that a deal with no customer contact in 21 days drops a stage.
Walked the reps through it and kept the acronym to one letter shorter than Gordie wanted.

decisions.choice: Write the stage rules from the closed-deal review, not from the textbook
decisions.why: Eighty deals gave reasons that could be tallied, so the playbook could rank the signals.
In the review, most late slips had gone quiet for three weeks before anyone noticed.

desk-drawer-co.context: Students at Brindle Hollow College and two other Harlow Ridge colleges wanted decent notebooks and pens without hunting through shops, and parents liked paying a fixed amount each month. A friend and I started Desk Drawer Co in September 2019, in our first year.
desk-drawer-co.problem: Handing over boxes on campus was cheap. What we did not know was whether the model survived once most orders came from out of town and went by post.
desk-drawer-co.my_role: Co-founder; ran sourcing, packing and finance
what_i_did: Bought notebooks, pens and sticky notes in bulk from a paper wholesaler and packed every box by hand.
Sold at a monthly campus handover day and through a small web shop, logging orders in Google Sheets and later Shopify.
Worked out margin per box each month, separately for campus handover and posted boxes.
The colleges shut in 2020 and handover days ended. For six months we posted nearly everything, and costs rose again.
Wound it up in June 2021 after settling every supplier and helper, then shared a candid write-up of the figures.

decisions.choice: Keep campus handover free and charge for postage
decisions.why: Handover boxes made $3.10 each; posted boxes lost money. Charging $4 for postage cut posted orders by a third.

decisions.choice: Wind down rather than raise money
decisions.why: Growth could only come from posted boxes, and each lost $2.60 after replacements and returns. Fresh funding would simply have lost money faster.

results.note: after postage, packaging and 9% replacements; arithmetic

desk-drawer-co.learned: I should have split margin by channel in month one. For most of a year we cheered growth that came from the channel losing money.
